legacy_versions.reader_title: Why EU privacy law makes scraping data for AI training far harder than US law
legacy_versions.reader_what: Scraping public personal data is broadly permissible in the US but rarely justifiable under the GDPR.
legacy_versions.reader_why: The gap shapes where firms can lawfully source training data for AI models.
legacy_versions.reader_more: The authors compare how United States and European Union privacy rules treat the mass collection of web data used to train AI models. They conclude that in the US the decisive question is whether the data was publicly accessible, while in the EU public availability is not enough on its own. Under the GDPR a scraper still needs a lawful basis under Article 6, which the authors think will almost never be satisfied in practice. They also observe that national data protection authorities have enforced this unevenly, so the practical position differs between member states. They argue privacy law should be reformed to reconcile the two aims rather than left as it stands.

deep_analysis.research_question: Whether scraping data to train AI models is lawful under US and EU data privacy law.
deep_analysis.main_finding: Public accessibility largely legitimises scraping in the US, whereas the GDPR's lawful-basis test makes scraping of personal data very hard to justify in the EU, though enforcement varies by member state.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Doctrinal legal analysis comparing existing US and EU privacy instruments, centred on GDPR Article 6.
deep_analysis.qualification: A doctrinal reading of the law rather than empirical evidence about scraping practice or enforcement outcomes; the reform proposal is the authors' own recommendation.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Directly concerns the legal conditions under which European AI developers can assemble training data.

legacy_versions.reader_what: Transfers did not robustly reduce regional entrapment risk, while higher research spending consistently did.
legacy_versions.reader_why: Suggests current allocation may underserve the low research-intensity regions most at risk.
legacy_versions.reader_more: This paper tests whether European Cohesion Policy fiscal transfers reduce the risk that EU regions fall into a development trap, meaning prolonged stagnation relative to peers. It uses a regression discontinuity design with heterogeneous treatment effects over 2000 to 2020, exploiting eligibility thresholds to approximate a causal comparison. The results do not robustly confirm a direct role for the transfers in reducing entrapment risk. Regions with higher research and development spending, however, consistently show reduced risk, which the author reads as evidence that such spending sustains long-term productivity and growth. The conclusion drawn is that the current fund allocation strategy may inadequately support regions with low research intensity and should be reassessed.

deep_analysis.qualification: Cross-sectional associations rather than causal estimates; the absence of an aggregate effect does not establish that innovation outputs have none, and the anchor institution role is inferred from group differences.

link:https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijmedinf..reader_more: This structured narrative review tests the 2020 EIT Health and McKinsey forecast against evidence through 2025, classifying each prediction as realised, under-realised, exceeded or unanticipated. link:https://doi.org/10.1177/09504222261.reader_what: PhD students prefer remaining in Italy despite poor pay and scarce vacancies; salary is not decisive.

link:https://publications.jrc.ec.europa..reader_what: Modelling suggests shifting research from yield maximisation to input saving could cut chemical use substantially.
link:https://publications.jrc.ec.europa..reader_more: This study evaluates long-term prospects for sustainable agricultural productivity growth under different assumptions about public agricultural research spending, treating that spending as the key productivity driver. It also asks what happens if research focus shifts from maximising yield towards technologies that save inputs such as fertilisers and pesticides. link:https://doi.org/10.1057/s41307-026-.reader_more: This paper argues that an emerging new cold war has produced a neo-academic cold war, structurally different from the last one. Where the previous era featured bipolar US-Soviet competition with separate scientific ecosystems, the author describes today's as multipolar, with semi-autonomous silos of transnational science cooperation and science diplomacy. He traces this to a sequence of global shocks: the September 2001 attacks, war and economic displacement, the rise of neonationalism and illiberal democracies, Russia and China re-emerging as adversaries to the US and EU, Brexit, the pandemic, and the second Trump presidency. He identifies China and Europe as beneficiaries of declining American scientific capability and protectionism, and open science and global problem-solving capacity as the losers.

link:https://doi.org/10.1007/s10796-026-.reader_what: Higher cyber-risk awareness correlates with fewer cybercrime incidents among European SMEs; more training raises reported incidents.
link:https://doi.org/10.1007/s10796-026-.reader_why: SMEs are Europe's weakest cybersecurity link, so detection and culture shape industrial digital resilience.
link:https://doi.org/10.1007/s10796-026-.reader_more: The study draws on a 2021 survey of more than 12,000 representative respondents from small and medium-sized enterprises across Europe. Firms reporting greater awareness of cyber risk recorded fewer cybercrime incidents, while firms that had done more cybersecurity training reported more. The authors read this as better detection, or as responses that are reactive rather than preventive, and they also find greater digitalisation associated with more incidents. legacy_versions.reader_more: This study analyses cybercrime experience among European small and medium-sized firms using a 2021 dataset of more than 12,000 representative respondents. link:https://doi.org/10.1163/15691497-20.reader_what: Argues European subordination to NATO prevented the EU-CELAC summit from addressing structural asymmetries.

link:https://doi.org/10.1163/15691497-20.reader_more: This article advances an explicitly anti-imperialist reading of relations between the EU and Latin America and the Caribbean. The author's thesis is that NATO geopolitics, characterised as the strategic arm of United States power, is the primary factor conditioning those relations, producing a contradiction with the region's stated interest in autonomous development and its proclamation as a zone of peace. She argues the fourth EU-CELAC summit demonstrated this, reflecting an inability to question United States military intervention in the Caribbean or to change structural mechanisms such as trade agreements that she says perpetuate asymmetry and technological dependence. The conclusion urges the EU to distance itself from NATO. This is a strongly normative polemic rather than a neutral analysis, and its framing is contested.

legacy_versions.reader_more: This preprint studies how scarce computing is allocated across federated digital research infrastructure, combining a landscape review of UK and international practice including EuroHPC, a mechanism-design model of allocation under strategic user reports, and simulation on a public workload trace. Three findings recur. First, allocation records measure occupancy, meaning resources reserved, rather than utilisation, meaning useful work done, so funders cannot currently answer whether resources deliver productive value. Second, simple transparent scheduling heuristics perform close to a full-information benchmark once tuned, so the near-term opportunity is instrumenting existing schedulers rather than replacing them. Third, unmanaged federation behaves like uncoordinated routing, minimising average delay while concentrating load on receiving systems, analogous to Braess's paradox in road networks.

link:https://fiia.fi/wp-content/uploads/.reader_what: Paper argues the EU's growth model relies on externally sourced inputs and technologies, leaving it structurally fragile.
link:https://fiia.fi/wp-content/uploads/.reader_more: Strategic capitalism here describes an environment in which industrial policy, investment screening and export controls have become ordinary instruments of statecraft. The authors argue that Europe's current model, built on externally sourced inputs, technologies and infrastructures, is fragile under those conditions, and that its innovation future depends on aligning competitiveness with control over critical economic flows and a clear direction for innovation. They set out four trajectories: Dependent Europe, innovation without control or direction; Fortress Europe, control without dynamism; Fragmented Europe, ambition without alignment; and Strategic Europe, which aligns all three and is the only one they see leading to sustained technological leadership. The scenarios are analytical constructions used to structure the argument rather than predictions.

link:https://doi.org/10.1007/s40821-026-.reader_title: Corporate research units patent more green technology when the surrounding region already does
link:https://doi.org/10.1007/s40821-026-.reader_what: Across 118 European regions, host-region green innovation intensity predicts more green patents by resident corporate research units.
link:https://doi.org/10.1007/s40821-026-.reader_more: The sample covers 231 leading corporate research spenders with inventive activity spread across 118 European regions between 2000 and 2018. Using fixed-effects logistic and Poisson models, with a control function approach to address reverse causation, the authors find that higher green innovation intensity in a host region is associated with both whether and how many green patents the local research unit files. The association holds only under specific conditions: the host region is foreign to the firm, lies in Europe's core, is environmentally polluting, and regulates more strictly than the firm's home country. Knowledge in the region itself, rather than activity in neighbouring regions, drives the pattern. Patents measure inventive output imperfectly and the data end in 2018.

legacy_versions.reader_more: The Narrative Policy Framework breaks a policy story into four parts: characters, plot, setting and moral. The authors applied it to eighteen European Parliament documents from 2020 to 2024, manually coding 500 narratives, and found plots of control and of rising dominating, populated by heroes and beneficiaries rather than villains, presenting AI as both manageable and beneficial. legacy_versions.reader_what: Analysis finds EU food policy internally incoherent, incremental farm policy reform insufficient, and just-transition governance underdeveloped.

legacy_versions.reader_more: The authors combine participatory foresight with two structured techniques: the X-curve, which sequences the decline of an old system against the rise of a new one, and morphological analysis, which tests whether policy options can be consistently combined. The authors note that fully sequenced roadmaps remain for later work, and the evidence base is two expert workshops.

link:https://doi.org/10.1186/s40309-026-.reader_why: Gives analysts a way to match foresight method choice to the governing system it must serve.
link:https://doi.org/10.1186/s40309-026-.reader_more: The article rejects the view that foresight methods are transferable tools chosen mainly by object, horizon or data, and builds a framework linking methods to institutional functions across four governance logics: technocratic, market-managerial, networked and anticipatory. The EU is the focal case of institutionalised foresight in a multi-level system, with Japan and South Korea as contrastive cases. Evidence combines exploratory bibliometric mapping of Scopus, VOSviewer semantic analysis of foresight-method terms, manual validation of 68 publications and qualitative case interpretation. Findings place the EU as the most developed combination of networked and anticipatory functions, citing Strategic Foresight Reports, ESPAS and the EU-wide Foresight Network. The design is contrastive, not a symmetrical country comparison.

deep_analysis.qualification: Contrastive case design rather than a symmetrical comparison; the secondary cases are used illustratively.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Provides a transferable framework for analysing foresight capability, with EU foresight institutions as the focal case.

legacy_versions.reader_why: Addresses why foresight struggles for epistemic authority when set against established disciplines in policymaking.
legacy_versions.reader_more: Perspectival realism is a position in philosophy of science holding that knowledge advances through interaction between distinct epistemic communities, each working with its own models. The author borrows it to argue that foresight produces what he calls modal models, structured accounts of what is possible, which can legitimately sit alongside other forms of evidence in policy. From deliberative democracy he takes the emphasis on pluralism and on giving reasons, presenting this as what lends foresight depth in public debate rather than merely generating options. The paper is a theoretical contribution: it offers a justification for foresight's standing in the policy process rather than evidence that adopting this framing changes practice.

legacy_versions.reader_what: Paper proposes analysing what a technology does, rather than what it is called, to detect emerging technologies.

legacy_versions.reader_more: Functional analysis asks what function an artefact performs for a user, instead of describing it by its components or its label. The authors apply that lens to technology foresight, combining it with natural language processing tuned for patent documents and with expert domain knowledge. They use it to look for development patterns, spot missing elements and potential failure points, and to strengthen conventional bibliometric approaches such as S-curve analysis. Their affordability argument rests on patent and publication data being cheap and widely available, so the constraint is analytical capacity rather than access. This is a 2016 methodological proposal demonstrated by its own authors, and the text-mining techniques available have changed substantially since.

link:https://doi.org/10.1002/pan3.70388.reader_title: A framework for making coherent design choices when building biodiversity scenarios
link:https://doi.org/10.1002/pan3.70388.reader_what: The authors develop and validate a framework aligning scenario design choices with the question a scenario is meant to answer.
link:https://doi.org/10.1002/pan3.70388.reader_why: Incoherent scenario design risks missing important policy-relevant risks and opportunities.
link:https://doi.org/10.1002/pan3.70388.reader_more: Decision-makers face pressure to act transformatively on biodiversity loss, and scenarios are used to explore alternative futures and the outcomes of possible actions. The authors argue that amid considerable methodological diversity there is little guidance on the range of scenario design choices available or their suitability for particular applications. The contribution is methodological guidance for scenario builders; it is demonstrated on biodiversity applications, and its wider transferability is argued rather than tested across domains.

link:https://doi.org/10.1002/ffo2.70043.reader_why: Foresight methods lose diagnostic value when transplanted into administrative scoring routines.
link:https://doi.org/10.1002/ffo2.70043.reader_more: Methods such as net assessment, scenarios and Black Swan thinking travel across countries and institutions, and change on the way. This article builds an evaluative case study around Indonesia's 2025 national resilience planning to ask when such changes are sensible local adaptation and when the method has been stretched past the point where it still does its job. The procedure has three stages and uses explicit decision rules, so it can be applied to other documents and settings. Empirically, exploratory methods were found to have been recast as periodic categorisation and prioritisation. The author does not claim this changed policy outcomes.

deep_analysis.research_question: Are divergences in how foresight methods are operationalised in Indonesian resilience planning adaptation or conceptual stretching?
deep_analysis.main_finding: Exploratory and diagnostic foresight methods were consistently translated into an operational regime of commensuration, scoring and classificatory closure.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Three-stage coded document analysis of official policy documents against specified reference purposes, boundary conditions and evidential expectations.
deep_analysis.qualification: No causal claim about policy outcomes; conclusions are bounded propositions, and full text could not be legitimately accessed.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Supplies a reusable evaluation procedure for foresight method quality and fidelity.

link:https://doi.org/10.1002/ffo2.70042.reader_title: A method for long-range foresight built on synchronising nested historical cycles
link:https://doi.org/10.1002/ffo2.70042.reader_what: Proposes that five nested social and technological cycles converge roughly every 250 years into a civilisational epoch.
link:https://doi.org/10.1002/ffo2.70042.reader_why: Extends foresight beyond near-term trend analysis toward structured long-range anticipation.
link:https://doi.org/10.1002/ffo2.70042.reader_more: Most foresight looks a decade or two ahead. This article proposes a method for looking much further. It synthesises five nested cycles — from decadal innovation waves up to century-long institutional rhythms — and argues that they periodically fall into step, producing what the author calls a Mega Epoch about every 250 years. The method is demonstrated by mapping 2,500 years of Western history into ten such epochs, drawing on macrohistorians including Ibn Khaldun, Toynbee, Kondratieff, Strauss and Howe, and Turchin. The author states the framework is non-deterministic, open to falsification, and dependent on assumptions such as stable generation length.

deep_analysis.main_finding: Nested cycles are argued to converge at roughly 250-year intervals, yielding a Ten Mega Epochs mapping of Western history.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Synthesis of five cycle traditions into a single temporal framework, applied retrospectively across 2,500 years.
deep_analysis.qualification: Explicitly non-deterministic and contingent on stable retroactive structures; the demonstration is retrospective, not predictive validation.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: A transferable long-range foresight methodology usable independently of the demonstration case.

link:https://doi.org/10.1007/s11135-026-.reader_title: Hybrid Futures Triangle and fuzzy prioritisation framework for banking transformation under constraint
link:https://doi.org/10.1007/s11135-026-.reader_what: Sixty transformation drivers were scored and reduced to three futures: inertia, managed transition, transformational leap.
link:https://doi.org/10.1007/s11135-026-.reader_more: Financial systems under heavy institutional and geopolitical constraint are hard to forecast with conventional tools. This study builds a foresight framework around the Futures Triangle, which sets future-oriented goals against present pressures and inherited institutional limits. It adds a fuzzy multi-criteria step that scores candidate drivers on importance, uncertainty and rate of change, making the reduction from a long driver list to a working set explicit rather than tacit. Sixty drivers were drawn from expert interviews, regulatory papers and international foresight reports, producing three configurations for Iran's banking sector. The framework is the transferable part; the Iranian application is the demonstration.

link:https://doi.org/10.1108/fs-08-2025-.reader_title: Case study of why participatory foresight is hard to institutionalise in Peruvian regional planning

link:https://doi.org/10.1108/fs-08-2025-.reader_more: Peru has written participatory foresight into national planning rules, so it is a useful place to ask whether formal adoption translates into practice. The paper is a diagnosis of uptake conditions rather than a methodological contribution, which is why it falls outside the reusable-methods strand.

link:https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27029.reader_title: Expert foresight study on how AI unsettles the assumptions behind open-data governance
link:https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27029.reader_what: Generative AI breaks the visibility, institutional control and human-reader premises that open-data policy was built on.
link:https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27029.reader_why: Data governance frameworks may fail quietly if their founding assumptions no longer hold.
link:https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27029.reader_more: Two decades of open-data policy assumed that reuse is visible and traceable, that institutions keep meaningful control over information flows, and that humans read the data. This paper argues generative and inferential AI breaks all three: data disappears into opaque training pipelines, sensitive knowledge can be generated without touching the underlying dataset, and machines are becoming the main producers and consumers of information. The findings come from two expert forecasting studios convened by The GovLab in 2025-2026 with nineteen senior practitioners across statistics, trade policy, open science, AI governance and geospatial systems, whose elicited signals were clustered and stress-tested. Seven convergent signals are identified.

deep_analysis.qualification: Expert-elicited signals, not measured outcomes; the panel is small and self-selected, and the work is a preprint without peer review.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Method status is the open question: the authors frame their approach as applying established horizon-scanning practice, but the studio design is specified replicably.

link:https://doi.org/10.1016/j.futures.2.reader_more: Foresight is fundamentally about creating, circulating and applying knowledge about the future, so knowledge management ought to have a lot to say about it.
